INITIAL_EXPLORATION.name: INITIAL_EXPLORATION
INITIAL_EXPLORATION.objective: Understand how individual objects affect the detector.
guidelines: Observe detector responses as you place and remove objects
Pay attention to what changes when each object is added or removed
Notice any patterns in activation timing or sequence
With more objects, prioritize efficient exploration — focus on narrowing down which objects matter

COMBINATION_TESTING.name: COMBINATION_TESTING
COMBINATION_TESTING.objective: Discover how object combinations and arrangements affect activation.
guidelines: Test different groupings of objects on the detector
Vary not just which objects are present, but how you arrange and sequence them
Compare results across different configurations
If a configuration that should work doesn't, consider what else might matter

transitions.condition: If results are confusing, go back to singles

HYPOTHESIS_EVALUATION.name: HYPOTHESIS_EVALUATION
HYPOTHESIS_EVALUATION.objective: Evaluate your evidence to determine the causal rule.
guidelines: What rule type best explains ALL your observations?
Which specific objects are blickets?
Are there observations that don't fit your current hypothesis?
If observations are inconsistent, consider whether factors beyond object identity might matter

transitions.condition: When you have a clear hypothesis
If hypothesis is unclear, test more combinations

VERIFICATION.name: VERIFICATION
VERIFICATION.objective: Confirm your hypothesis with targeted tests before submitting.
guidelines: Design a test that would distinguish your hypothesis from the next most likely alternative
If the test confirms, submit your answer
If the test disconfirms, reconsider your hypothesis

DIMENSION_DISCOVERY.name: DIMENSION_DISCOVERY
DIMENSION_DISCOVERY.objective: The standard conjunctive/disjunctive framework doesn't explain your observations. Consider alternative causal dimensions: order of placement, probabilistic activation, or changing rules.
guidelines: Review ALL observations for patterns beyond which objects are present
Consider: does the ORDER of placement matter?
Consider: is activation PROBABILISTIC (same setup, different results)?
Consider: has the RULE CHANGED over time?
Form a new hypothesis about the causal mechanism

transitions.condition: Test new hypothesis with targeted experiments
If new hypothesis is clear enough to verify

ORDER_TESTING.name: ORDER_TESTING
ORDER_TESTING.objective: Determine the exact placement order required for activation. This is a systematic elimination task: there are a finite number of possible orderings, and you must test them one by one until you find the one that activates the detector.
guidelines: STEP 1: List all objects you believe are relevant based on the evidence so far (e.g., from environmental observations and your own testing)
STEP 2: Calculate how many possible orderings exist. For 3 objects there are exactly 6 orderings. For 4 objects there are exactly 24 orderings. Write out ALL possible orderings explicitly
STEP 3: For each test — clear the detector completely, then place objects ONE AT A TIME in a specific sequence, then check. Record the result: 'Tested [X, Y, Z] → INACTIVE' or '→ ACTIVE'
STEP 4: After each failed test, cross that ordering off your list. Choose the NEXT UNTESTED ordering from your list. Never repeat an ordering you have already tested
STEP 5: Continue until you find the activating order or exhaust all possibilities. If all orderings fail, your object set may be wrong — go back and reconsider which objects are relevant
IMPORTANT: Do NOT guess based on alphabetical order, intuition, or pattern-matching. The correct order could be ANY permutation. Only an ordering you have TESTED and seen ACTIVATE is confirmed
IMPORTANT: Work through orderings methodically. A good strategy is to fix the first object and cycle through all arrangements of the remaining objects before moving to the next first object

transitions.condition: ONLY after you have tested an ordering that produced ACTIVE — submit that specific ordering
If ALL orderings of your current object set fail, your object set is wrong — go back and revise which objects are in the rule
